decisions.quote: Given that our study used similar methodology as Sparks and Barclay (2013) [23], we can conclude that we failed to replicate the eyes effect in this study. Participants did not report feeling more observed in the presence of eyes and did not give more money in a dictator game when images of eyes were present compared to the control condition.
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from a fresh sample of 355 university students playing a dictator game across Public, Eyes, and No-Eyes control conditions, adapting the methodology of Sparks and Barclay (2013) [23] to re-test the watching eyes effect on generosity. Because new data were collected to re-test a specific published finding, both shipped and blind codings are right that the type is replication.

corrected_value.title: Altruism and indirect reciprocity: The interaction of person and situation in prosocial behavior

decisions.location: Goal and Hypotheses, line 9; Results (Exploratory Analyses: Simplified Conditions), line 42; Discussion, lines 52-53; References, Ref. 39, line 185
decisions.quote: To simplify comparisons, we combined the eyes and no-eyes control conditions into a single private condition to determine if individual differences in SVO influenced dictator game allocations when decisions were anonymous (i.e., private) or not (i.e., public). This analysis was not pre-registered, and can be considered exploratory, or as a replication of Simpson & Willer (2008;[39]).
decisions.reason: The primary source explicitly states in its Goal and Hypotheses (line 9), Results (line 42), Discussion (lines 52-53), and Supplementary Material (line 69) that it conducts an empirical replication of Simpson and Willer (2008) (Reference 39, Social Psychology Quarterly 71(1):37-52) in new sample data (n=189 participants with SVO data), testing whether Social Value Orientation (egoists vs. prosocials) differentially predicts dictator game allocations across private (anonymous) versus public conditions and running an equivalence test against Simpson and Willer's effect size (d = 0.39). This is a completely distinct original work and finding from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2502, Sparks & Barclay 2013, Evolution and Human Behavior, doi: 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2013.05.001, which tested the watching-eyes effect under short exposure). No DOI is printed in the source for Reference 39. Prior adjudication/state files do not exist for this work.
